title: The Starry Night
summary: The Starry Night is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just before sunrise, with the addition of an imaginary village. It has been in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1941, acquired through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest. Described as a "touchstone of modern art", The Starry Night has been regarded as one of the most recognizable paintings in the Western canon.

sections.name: The Swirling Sky
sections.description: The dominant feature of the painting, featuring stylized blue swirls and luminous yellow stars. It represents the turbulent emotional energy Van Gogh perceived in the night sky.

sections.name: The Crescent Moon
sections.description: A bright, glowing orange-yellow crescent moon in the top right corner. It is a focal point of light and warmth against the cool tones of the night.

sections.name: The Cypress Tree
sections.description: A tall, dark, flame-like cypress tree on the left. In the late 19th century, these trees were symbols of mourning and mortality, providing a somber balance to the sky.

sections.name: The Village and Church
sections.description: A quiet village with a prominent church spire at the base of the mountains. This part of the scene was imaginary, likely inspired by the architecture of Van Gogh's homeland.

museum_facts: Van Gogh painted this oil on canvas in June 1889 while staying at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy.
The sky is dominated by a bright moon on the right and Venus near the center-left.
Though inspired by the view from his asylum window, the village came from other views, and the cypress is shown much closer than it was.
Van Gogh painted this nighttime scene in several sessions during the day, using vivid blues and yellows to heighten its expressive mood.

guide_notes.The Swirling Sky: Under your fingertips the upper part of the relief rolls in long, continuous ridges that curve across the surface like slow waves, one band folding into the next without a single straight line to follow. Feel how the raised strokes are short and slightly ridged, laid side by side and sometimes overlapping, so the whole field feels combed and restless rather than smooth. This is the night sky, which fills about three-quarters of the painting and presses down toward the quiet town below. The waves are not cloud or smoke but paint: Van Gogh built them from countless short brushstrokes laid on thickly, and pigment analysis has confirmed he mixed ultramarine and cobalt blue to make this deep, agitated field.
guide_notes.The Crescent Moon: Move to the upper right corner and you will find a bright, raised crescent, a thin sliver with a broad open curve, sitting inside a wide circular disc of concentric rings. Trace outward from the crescent's point and your finger crosses ring after ring of slightly raised arcs, like ripples spreading from a dropped stone. The crescent and its rings are the brightest, warmest-touched area of the relief, standing out against the cooler surrounding sky. Van Gogh's moon is deliberately not astronomically accurate, records show the real moon was waning gibbous that June, and one scholar proposed the glowing halo may be a leftover of the fuller moon he first intended to paint.
guide_notes.The Cypress Tree: At the left foreground a tall dark form rises almost the full height of the relief, close enough that your fingers can trace it as a single vertical mass. It tapers and twists upward like a flame, its edges broken into short wavy strokes rather than a clean outline, and it is markedly taller and nearer than anything around it. This is a cypress tree, painted in deep burnt umber and blue-black, and it stands as a bridge between the earthbound town and the spinning sky. In Mediterranean tradition the cypress is a tree of graveyards and mourning; Van Gogh called them beautiful of line and compared their proportions to an Egyptian obelisk.
guide_notes.The Village and Church: Now run your fingers along the lower third of the relief, where the surface turns calm and orderly after the sky. Feel the low blocky shapes of small houses packed close together, each outlined with a firmer ridge, and rising from among them a single pointed spire that juts up sharply into the hills behind. A few tiny, slightly raised rectangles suggest lit windows, and the spire is the one feature that pierces the skyline. This village could not actually be seen from Van Gogh's asylum window, he based it on a sketch made from a hillside, and the steeple is more Dutch than Provencal, echoing the churches of his childhood.
